site.title: Grok Bot Tips Watch
site.tagline: Searchable reference of Grok Bot and AI coding tips from 16 builders on X
site.scope_short: Grok Bot, Cursor, agent skills, prompting and AI coding workflows
site.scope_about: Grok Bot and other AI tools (coding agents, Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, agent skills, prompting and workflows)

runs.window: restructure: subcategories, editions, source cards (no new content)
runs.note: Two tips that only pointed at their own video were folded into the video source cards.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Build and own a custom review agent
tips.tip: Write a review agent that enforces your own architecture, PII handling and style rules rather than relying only on off-the-shelf reviewers.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Review in a fresh context, not self-review
tips.tip: Hand the diff to a separate reviewer sub-agent in a fresh context window. In the Warp benchmark shown, an independent reviewer averaged 71.1% correctness at $12.02 vs 68.6% at $4.82 for self-review.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Make the reviewer return structured JSON
tips.tip: Have the reviewer output a verdict ("approved" / "needs changes" / "requires human input") plus findings with line/blocks, a suggestion and severity ("nit" / "important" / "critical").

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Run the agent review loop before opening the PR
tips.tip: Keep implement/review iterations inside your agent platform so GitHub isn't cluttered with bot comments.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Cap implement/review rounds at about 3-5
tips.tip: Limit the agent implement-and-review loop to roughly 3-5 turns.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Verify end to end in a sandbox via Chrome DevTools Protocol
tips.tip: A "Test Desktop App" skill boots the Electron app in a container (factory.yaml: os linux, arch x86_64, dockerImage warpdotdev/dev-base:latest) and drives it through the Chrome DevTools Protocol.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Have the agent record its test session as an MP4
tips.tip: Give reviewers a video of the agent's verification run.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Add a merge-risk skill to every PR
tips.tip: Score the PR on Alignment, Impact, Verification, Rollback cost and Error detection, and append a low/medium/high risk rating to the PR description.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Benchmark new models on your own past agent tasks
tips.tip: When a new model comes out, don't rely on SOTA benchmark numbers: rerun it against your own previous agent tasks to compare cost and quality, and switch only if it measures up. That's why factories should be measurable and model-agnostic.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Benchmark several model configs in one run on the same harness
tips.tip: Put multiple model configurations (e.g. Gemini 4 Carbon vs Gemini 4 Argon) in a single benchmark run on the same harness.

tips.author: owickstrom
tips.title: Review diffs with diffview-plus.nvim + jj
tips.tip: For code review, @owickstrom recommends diffview-plus.nvim combined with jj (Jujutsu).

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Use a Home Repo to run agents across many repos
tips.tip: A Home Repo is one repository holding your shared skills, AGENTS.md and shared docs; you start agent sessions there, and its AGENTS.md has one-line pointers to each other repo (path, plus where to clone it from if missing). Repo-specific docs and commands stay in each repo. Matt's article includes a copy-paste setup prompt that inventories your repos and skills, asks you decisions in rounds, and changes nothing until you approve. Past ~20 repos, point to one file per business area instead.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Put private skills and shared settings in the Home Repo
tips.tip: Keep private skills (sensitive workflows) and version-controlled config like settings.json in the Home Repo so the whole team gets them.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Keep custom CLI tooling in the Home Repo
tips.tip: E.g. one CLI wrapping Slack, Discord, GitHub and Google Calendar for your agents. The Home Repo can also hold an LLM wiki of markdown on audiences, business concepts and architecture (05:44).

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: A string of prompts isn't a factory
tips.tip: In Zach's experience with customers, chaining cloud agents with prompts doesn't scale. Companies want resilient, measurable, configurable, low-latency factories with audit logs and security guarantees: the same production quality as their products.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Delegate whole workstreams, not just personal errands
tips.tip: Grok Bot isn't just a personal agent: treat it as a teammate you can hand full workstreams to and let it run them end to end. Grok Bot 1.0 added sharing bots, working with them in Slack and Teams, and inviting them to meetings.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Pull a bot into a video call from chat
tips.tip: Invite a bot to a video call from text chat and it joins.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Have bots tag each other to hand off work
tips.tip: Bots can tag one another in channels to pass work along (e.g. a research bot handing off to a copy bot).

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Use a bot as a safety net before sharing
tips.tip: Bots can warn you about sensitive content, e.g. confidential financials on slides, before a deck is shared externally.

tips.author: EnoReyes
tips.title: Bugs found are a floor, not a count
tips.tip: If your Droid (Factory's agent) finds 2 bugs in your code, the best estimate of how many bugs there are is not 2.

tips.author: ccheever
tips.title: Let agents verify mobile changes on cloud simulators
tips.tip: Expo Simulators are cloud simulators/emulators built for agents: the agent runs its change on one and brings back a recording before asking for your attention, which helps when agents write mobile code faster than a team can review.

tips.author: ccheever
tips.title: Let agents check UI across device types, with a human pause
tips.tip: Expo Simulators work from local and cloud agents (00:25), let agents test UI across iPhones, Androids, foldables and watches, and the workflow can pause for a human to check the simulator before the agent ships (00:50).

tips.author: cursor_ai
tips.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen in Cursor: 54.3% on CursorBench
tips.tip: Gemini 4 Hydrogen is available in Cursor. At default effort it scores 54.3% on CursorBench (vs 39.6% for Gemini 3.8 Flash), priced at $1.50/M input and $7.50/M output tokens. Compare every effort level at cursor.com/evals.

tips.author: Baconbrix
tips.title: Run Grok Bot on a Mac to reach Apple apps from anywhere
tips.tip: Grok Bot on Mac can use Messages, Mail, Notes, Reminders, Calendar, Location and Contacts. You can then remote-control that Mac from any Grok Bot client (mobile, web, Tesla) to check your calendar, send messages, or read reminders.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Prefill bot messages from links and shortcuts
tips.tip: Grok Bot supports deep links that open your bot with a message already drafted. Put one in a shortcut, a note, or another app. Build your own with the deep-links docs at docs.x.ai/grok-bot/deep-links.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Prefill links come in web and app forms
tips.tip: Shareable prefilled-prompt links work as a web link (https://cursor.com/grok-bot/link/v1/prompt?text=...) or an app link (grokbot://app/v1/prompt?text=...).

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Treat coding agents as an engineering problem, not a prompting problem
tips.tip: Core idea of Zach's AIE Code keynote: define the agent system in code, measure what it produces on your codebase, and keep iterating. Everyone has agents; the hard part is engineering the factory around them.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Connect more apps so your bot has context
tips.tip: The more connectors (and so context and tools) a bot has, the more useful it gets. Two starter ideas: have it read messages from family and put important events on your calendar, or read messages from prospective clients and manage your small-business bookings.

tips.author: ccheever
tips.title: Fast cloud iOS builds and instant sharing with Exact Build + AppDrop
tips.tip: If you're trying Exact: Exact Build is a fast (Linux-based) iOS build service, often under 30 seconds, and AppDrop signs and distributes IPAs so you can send what you built to someone's iPhone right away. Both are in alpha.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Blueprints plus an orchestrator agent, not rigid if-this-then-that
tips.tip: Warp's factory design: users define a workflow 'blueprint' that looks like a DAG, but an orchestration agent decides how to progress work and when to loop in a human, so it can take a different path when guidelines are incomplete or a human asks.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Swap walls of markdown for an /animatic video
tips.tip: Matt is building two skills: /setup-animatic (picks the tooling and sets it up locally or on a remote machine) and /animatic (creates an upload-ready video). The goal: every important PR comes with a video showing how it works.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: How /animatic turns a PR into a narrated video
tips.tip: The agent writes a JSON storyboard, Playwright renders code frames from the PR diff, TTS reads each line and FFmpeg stitches an MP4. Voice engine (ElevenLabs, OpenAI, Edge-TTS), rendering style and stitcher are CLI options (00:56); the MP4 is posted as a PR comment via the GitHub/GitLab API or saved locally (01:25).

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Keep the agent pipeline as version-controlled code
tips.tip: Defining the factory as code lets you branch to test configurations (e.g. are open-weight models fine for front-end tasks? are these skills worth their tokens?) and enables self-improvement loops where agents analyze past failures and propose diffs to the definition.

tips.author: Baconbrix
tips.title: Try shopping through the bot
tips.tip: Shopping with Grok Bot now delivers results as cards; after you order you get a progress card and the bot keeps an eye on the order automatically.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Ask Grok Bot questions inside the docs
tips.tip: The docs (docs.x.ai/grok-bot/overview) now have Grok Bot built in: it answers from the docs, links the pages it used, and can draw a diagram of how a task runs.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Ask the docs for a diagram
tips.tip: On supported docs pages, 'Ask Grok Bot' answers questions about the page; asking it to walk through how Grok Bot handles a task 'with a diagram' returns a step-by-step flowchart.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: The software factory stack, layer by layer
tips.tip: 00 factories-as-code (workflows, permissions, sandbox config all versioned); 01 own your data and context (skills, MCPs, traces, logs); 02 compute: agents get their own sandboxed, self-hostable computers; 03 inference: any model and harness, no lock-in; 04 improvement: observe cost per PR, cycle time and DORA metrics, with agents scoring output and proposing changes; 05 orchestration: launch, track, recover, pass messages; 06 access: MCP server/REST API and integrations (Slack, Teams, Jira, Linear) rather than a tightly coupled web 'ADE'.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Bring your bot to meetings so it gathers its own context
tips.tip: Inviting a bot to meetings lets it collect context firsthand, which makes it smarter over time. It can also attend for you (e.g. when you're on a flight without connectivity) and take notes. To set it up, just ask your bot.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Ask the bot for things out loud during meetings
tips.tip: Once in a Zoom/Google Meet call (ask it in chat to join), the bot responds to spoken requests such as sending follow-ups, confirms with a chat reaction, and writes structured notes and action items into apps like Notion (00:18).

tips.author: Baconbrix
tips.title: Say your blockers out loud on calls with the bot present
tips.tip: With Grok Bot in a work meeting, voice the things blocking you; the bot can follow up later with a ping when it finds a way to unblock you.

tips.author: GeoffreyHuntley
tips.title: Be skeptical of viral agent launches
tips.tip: Geoffrey gets about three paid-promotion offers a day; his rule of thumb is to assume a viral agent product was paid-boosted and look for honest reviews instead.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Quick fixes considered harmful: ask agents for the root-cause fix
tips.tip: Asking an agent for the smallest or quickest change can make it write worse code: the bandaid becomes a pattern the next agent copies until it spreads everywhere. We used to accept bandaids because time was short; agents change that calculus, so sometimes ask for the root-cause fix even if it's more invasive.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Keep reviewing something: plan, design, or result
tips.tip: The No AI Slop Manifesto (slopmanifesto.com), co-written at AIE Code Summit, says AI amplifies human judgment rather than replacing it; we own the intent, taste and consequences of what we ship; and there will always be value in reviewing something. Even if we stop reading most code, review the plan, design or result, or you get the same output as everyone else. The right level of review depends on the stakes.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Give runtime-verification skills a feature map
tips.tip: Runtime-verification skills include a 'feature map': a user-facing site map of the app's features, giving agents and humans shared vocabulary (so 'the thingy in the left sidebar' is unambiguous), plus reusable custom CLIs/drivers that save tokens and are testable.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Example outer loop: auto-fuzz every release with Grok Bot
tips.tip: On each new release, Grok Bot spins up a Cursor project that fuzzes the build like a real user, opens fix PRs for bugs it finds, and auto-merges them.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Guide agents with an inverted pyramid: deterministic first, prose last
tips.tip: Rely most on deterministic codebase design and static analysis (API design, architecture, lint rules, types, tests), then verification, and least on prose instructions (rules, skills, AGENTS.md) and human review.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Turn every agent correction into a deterministic check
tips.tip: When you correct an agent, or catch something in review, make the fix a lint rule or other deterministic check in the codebase rather than new text in an instructions markdown file. Agents copy the patterns they see, so keep bad patterns out of the code.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Enforce architecture with directory-based import bans
tips.tip: Encode boundaries in the directory structure and ban imports across them, e.g. code in electron-renderer can't import from electron-main.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Design foolproof APIs; ban nuanced ones like useEffect
tips.tip: APIs that need nuance to use well lead to slop. Design foolproof APIs and ban nuanced ones, such as React's useEffect in product code.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Stop agents writing unsolicited markdown docs
tips.tip: Agents use markdown and docs they weren't asked for to justify wrong implementations; stop them writing it.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Ban imperative quick fixes like setTimeout and requestAnimationFrame
tips.tip: Quick fixes spread: in the example shown, one agent's timer hack grew to 183 timers. Ban imperative timer-based patches such as setTimeout/requestAnimationFrame.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Treat code comments as liabilities
tips.tip: Comments aren't enforceable and agents use them to justify workarounds, so delete them. The team cut comments from 65,824 to 1,227 while growing to 169 lint rules.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Spend most agent tokens on verification, with an app CLI to drive the app
tips.tip: Put roughly 70% of agent token spend into verification. Give agents a CLI to drive and screenshot your app so they check their own work before human review, e.g. `app aria:click --accessible-name "Settings"`, `app snapshot`, `app screenshot proof.png`.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Model state machines with TLA+ and prove algorithms with Lean
tips.tip: Add formal verification as another layer: TLA+ to model state machines and Lean to prove algorithms.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Fuzz your UI with property-based testing (Bombadil)
tips.tip: Use property-based UI testing to fuzz the UI; the Grok Bot team uses Bombadil (github.com/antithesishq/bombadil).

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Generate statecharts and other visual artifacts for reviewers
tips.tip: Have agents produce visual artifacts such as statecharts so reviewers can check behavior quickly. The statechart skill is part of pstack (github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/pstack).

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Don't automate a low-trust loop
tips.tip: If your inner agent loop produces slop, automating it just produces more. Improve constraints and self-verification first.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Once the loop is high-trust, add an outer loop on triggers
tips.tip: With a trusted inner loop, add an outer loop that kicks off agents from Linear tickets, Slack messages, cron schedules, or Datadog/Sentry alerts.

tips.author: swyx
tips.title: Surface assumptions as editable widgets before generating
tips.tip: Feedforward UX: the AI shows its assumptions (e.g. kids' ages, interests) as editable controls before writing the plan, offers preselected style/color dropdowns for creative assets (00:26), and 'leaving blanks' templates for missing details like guest count or tone (00:41), so you steer without extra chat turns.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Pace AI output to human speed
tips.tip: Slow down. Pace AI outputs to human speeds; engineering still moves at engineering speed and business moves slower, and teams pushing too hard are starting to see downtime.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: AI writes the code; you still decide what ships
tips.tip: Revisiting an older post: senior engineers should build guardrails and teach practices that lead to quality software. AIs may write most of the code, but you decide what ships; don't lose your taste for quality.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: 'You are the long-term owner of this codebase': early benchmark notes
tips.tip: Early (10%-complete) SlopCodeBench run on Fable 5.2 comparing the standard 'just solve' prompt with Anthropic's recommended 'you are the long term owner of this codebase' addendum: the owner line roughly doubles tokens per task, but cost per pass is about the same; it tends to produce more formal tests; on circuit_eval it got a full pass vs 50% for the default. Unclear yet whether results are better overall.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Keep a dated llm-wiki of your audience in your Home Repo
tips.tip: Matt keeps an llm-wiki in his Home Repo that ingests good tweets, Discord/Slack messages, Gmail, YouTube and LinkedIn comments. Every claim is dated (or linked to a commit permalink) so it goes stale less. He uses it to answer questions like what people get confused about or what they're asking now, and frames it as an agent-friendly data structure built from existing data rather than 'memory'.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Remove nuance from agents' decisions (from @poteto's AIE talk)
tips.tip: 'Nuance tends to lead to slop.' Raise quality by designing APIs and automated checks that take nuance out of agents' choices: ban useEffect, ban ~99% of explanatory comments (they just lead to workarounds), and build APIs that hide complexity from agents.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Use a field's precise domain terms in prompts
tips.tip: Precise domain vocabulary pulls the relevant knowledge out of the model.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Tell the model which trade-offs matter
tips.tip: The model's first correct solution is rarely the best one; state the trade-offs that matter for your problem.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Give agents straight-line tasks toward a verifiable goal
tips.tip: Agents are strong tactically but weak at ambiguous design work that needs judgment; hand them clear tasks with a verifiable goal.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Avoid nuance in the APIs and codebases agents work in
tips.tip: Ambiguity leads agents to poor choices and slop.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Spend the time agents save on quality
tips.tip: Use the time saved on drudgery to raise quality, not just to ship more features.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Re-check agent code's assumptions as data grows
tips.tip: Trade-offs chosen early (e.g. for an empty database) can break as data grows; revisit them over time.

tips.author: owickstrom
tips.title: Run Antithesis from your coding agent
tips.tip: Antithesis launched a plugin that gives coding agents native access to Antithesis end to end, from system setup to test creation to debugging and validating fixes (example prompt: '/antithesis test HashiCorp Raft for bugs'), plus a self-serve Teams plan at $2,999/month.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: What a factory's orchestration layer must do
tips.tip: Once foundations are in code, orchestration should: read the code at the current version (or an experiment branch); spin up the right sandbox on demand; route work to agents with the right model and harness; prompt them per the factory code; store artifacts and traces; loop in humans who can hand off or steer; and integrate with Sentry, GitHub, Jira, Slack, etc. Think Terraform, but for agents.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Getting developers to adopt shared agent infrastructure
tips.tip: Frame the job as designing the factory, not working the assembly line. Expect friction when personal agent setups (harness, model, skills, MCPs) move to shared, team-owned cloud infrastructure defined in code; acknowledge it may feel like a step back, and pose it as a team engineering problem to solve together.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Send voice prompts straight to the agent
tips.tip: New in Cursor: voice prompts can go directly to the agent, without a separate click to dictate and another to send. Built by a self-described voice-prompting power user.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Edit dictated prompts before sending, including follow-ups
tips.tip: Click the mic in the agent prompt box to dictate (text transcribes live); cancel or stop recording and edit before sending. It works for follow-ups too, e.g. 'Write a unit test for the dark mode toggle' (00:22).

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: A prompt to evaluate any new technology against your codebase
tips.tip: Prompt of the day (using the XState v6 beta): 1) research what it does and the problem it solves; 2) find the gnarliest problem in our app it might help with; 3) build a proof of concept in a draft PR; 4) fully verify the results; 5) grade it on API nuance (more is worse; agents do better with fewer choices), type safety, testability, added cyclomatic complexity, docs quality, and deployment changes; 6) give an overall recommendation. Swap in any technology.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Constrain your tools with harsh lint rules (/constrain)
tips.tip: Experiment idea: if too much choice hurts agents, make extremely constrained versions of the tools you like, e.g. React allowed but all state must live in Zustand/useReducer, enforced by very strict lint rules, to strip out nuance and make the right path the only path.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Five tools to measure and improve agent throughput
tips.tip: 1) Online evals and LLM-as-judge scorers on past runs (e.g. 'is it writing redundant tests?'); 2) self-improvement loops that mine eval results for factory changes; 3) benchmarks that rerun tasks under different configs; 4) model routing based on those results; 5) A/B tests to prove changes going forward.

tips.author: swyx
tips.title: Want agent managers that own outcomes, not 'AI employees'
tips.tip: swyx on trialing Devin Bots for a week: what works is the next abstraction above single tasks: always-on, proactive agents that own outcomes, manage subagents, review themselves, and report via interactive artifacts rather than long chats. He handed off AEO, QA, cross-platform app porting, personal admin automation and video editing. Don't overpromise 'AI employees'.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Evaluate agents on multi-step iterative tasks
tips.tip: One-shot tests miss it: watch whether agents refactor and centralize code as requirements grow, or pile on workarounds.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Watch for library avoidance
tips.tip: Agents often rewrite provided libraries from scratch instead of using them.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Judge an agent-designed API by whether other agents can use it
tips.tip: LibraryDesignBench finds agent-designed libraries are often hard for other agents to use.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Python anti-patterns agents produce
tips.tip: Watch for Go-style (value, error) tuple returns in Python (21:20), catch-and-reraise at every layer instead of letting exceptions bubble up (22:20), and type(x) == T instead of isinstance() (24:25).

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: For big refactors, delete and reimplement from a new plan
tips.tip: For a big refactor or library swap, delete the old code and tests, have the agent write a new plan, and reimplement from scratch rather than editing in place.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Draw on an image to show the bot what to change
tips.tip: Releases 1.0.3 to 1.2.0: draw right on an image to show your bot what to change (1.0.3); X DMs appear as draft cards you approve before anything is sent, plus a gift concierge (1.1.0); redesigned flight results and a full hotel photo viewer with zoomable maps (1.2.0). Changelog: x.ai/changelog/bot.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Onboard your bot with a 10-minute voice brain dump
tips.tip: Give the bot your most ambitious, end-to-end tasks. The best way to brief it: use voice dictation and talk for about 10 minutes, walking it through your workflow as if onboarding a new hire. Before sending, ask it to restate what you said in its own words. Name the tools and apps you use so it asks to connect them, and ask it to save its own skills so it repeats the workflow exactly your way.

tips.author: swyx
tips.title: One persistent bot per project, each with its own memory
tips.tip: Teams now create dedicated bots per project; each has its own long-lived identity, memory bank and goals, and they can talk to each other when needed. Create a bot to manage a goal you'll work on across sessions and days instead of reusing one long session.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Bring agents to where the work already lives
tips.tip: Zach's view: local prompting in terminals still has a place in the inner loop, but it's usually better to bring agents to where work happens and context lives than to pull the work into your local environment.

tips.author: GeoffreyHuntley
tips.title: Generate property-based tests from both the spec and the code
tips.tip: In a paper across 25 agent-built apps, spec-driven property-based tests found 56 bugs that code-driven ones missed, and code-driven found 43 that spec-driven missed (59% of bugs found by only one approach). Setup: an agent writes invariants in plain English from the requirements, then turns them into property tests by reading the code. Use both.

tips.author: swyx
tips.title: Astra as a workflow automation model
tips.tip: swyx is daily-driving Astra and calls it the best workflow automation model he's used: it no longer gets stuck in loops and learns efficiently through compactions and skill writing. It runs much of Latent Space and AI Engineer's content publishing pipeline.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Step back before firing off many small agent changes
tips.tip: It's easy to run lots of small 'move this button' changes in parallel, but if you never step back to think deeply about what you're building, you get slop. Take a moment to work out the best path forward.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Choose the approach by change size
tips.tip: One-shot tiny changes; for big features, start with an alignment phase on domain language.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Grill first: let the agent question you before coding
tips.tip: A command like /grill-with-docs makes the agent ask you questions before it writes any code.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Keep a GLOSSARY.md of project terms
tips.tip: Agents write better code when they know your domain's nouns and verbs.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Record ADRs so agents don't undo past decisions
tips.tip: Architectural Decision Records tell the agent why past decisions were made.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Compact the planning chat into a spec and tickets
tips.tip: Before implementing, compact a long planning chat (/compact) into a clean spec and a list of tickets, then run /implement-spec.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Run /retro after a big generation
tips.tip: The agent reviews its own code against your standards for rule violations, scope creep and excess complexity.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Split a huge PR into stacked PRs
tips.tip: Have the agent break a big PR into smaller stacked PRs (e.g. schema, backend, UI) and review them one by one.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Prefer soft deletes when replacing an old system
tips.tip: Use a soft delete (e.g. an archived flag) instead of hard-deleting data, so you can revert.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Browse and publish community bots at grok-bot.directory
tips.tip: grok-bot.directory is a community directory to browse and install bots and apps others have built, or publish your own (submit at grok-bot.directory/submit; submissions to the official marketplace that weren't published are listed there too). One day in it had 1,200+ bots submitted and 7,000+ adds.

tips.author: Baconbrix
tips.title: Give travel bookings loose preferences, not exact specs
tips.tip: Grok Bot can book seats, rebook a missed connection, help with refunds, or watch for upgrades, often triggered automatically from email. Pro tip: state loose preferences (for example, that you prefer aisle seats and don't mind waiting longer) rather than exact details and it generally finds better options.

tips.author: Baconbrix
tips.title: Give travel requests themes and dates
tips.tip: Ask for specific flights (e.g. nonstop SFO to LAX) and pick from options in chat (00:05), or give themed preferences and dates (e.g. a desert hotel near Joshua Tree) to get bookable hotel options.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Automating anything: start with the goal, not the process
tips.tip: Automation is a goal plus a process. Don't confuse steps (filling a form, sending an email) with the goal; ask what the work is for (revenue, cost) and tell a new bot the goal it's responsible for. If you can't phrase the goal, ask the bot to interview you until you have one you're happy with.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Brain-dump the process, then make the bot restate it before acting
tips.tip: Voice-dictate everything about how you do the job: the usual steps, what you watch out for, the apps and tools used, how you check the work, where the inputs come from, and where feedback comes from. Then ask the bot to restate your goal and process in plain English and not start executing yet. Iterate a few times, then let it connect the tools it needs; optionally ask it to review the process against the goal for a better way.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Teach the bot your judgment with real examples, one question at a time
tips.tip: You make many decisions without noticing (which source to trust when two disagree, when a task is truly 'done'). Feed the bot a few real examples, including ones that went wrong, and ask it to interview you about how you decide, where information lives, how you check work, and when to ask for help, one question at a time, before automating.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Let bots improve themselves by giving them access to feedback
tips.tip: Give the bot the apps and data it needs to find feedback itself (email, social, Google/Yelp reviews) so it can propose process improvements. The more of your business is logged digitally, the better; the bot can even build you a simple app to log events. Consistent unique IDs (customer email, order number, part number) across tools let it cross-reference data.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Use routines so the bot works without you asking
tips.tip: Without a routine, a bot only works when asked. Decide what should trigger the work (an incoming email, a Slack/Teams message, or a schedule) and ask the bot to set up the routine so you stop being the bottleneck.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Install the Dr Eggbot v2 template to design bots for you
tips.tip: Dr Eggbot is a bot designer that creates bots for you. A new v2 template ships with new skills for automating work and life; it differs from the old one, so install v2 fresh and ask the old Eggbot to transfer anything you want to keep.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Lots of agent-written tests don't prove the system works
tips.tip: A large pile of agent-written lint rules, unit tests or e2e tests doesn't mean the system is good. Agents are goal-seeking and can reward-hack or measure the wrong thing, so without real insight into what's happening you can't tell whether your verification is worth anything.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Choose how each tool runs (1.2.3)
tips.tip: Grok Bot 1.2.3 lets you pick how each tool runs, reconnect accounts right from chat, and makes the bot reach for connectors before the browser.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Share a profile page of everything you've published
tips.tip: grok-bot.directory now has profiles: one page listing all your published bots and apps, with a link you can share or pin. Find yours in the account menu.

tips.author: cursor_ai
tips.title: Gemini 4 Neon in Cursor: new cost-performance frontier
tips.tip: Gemini 4 Neon is available in Cursor. At default effort it scores 63.7% on CursorBench 4.1 (vs 57.3% for Gemini 4 Hydrogen), priced at $3/M input and $15/M output tokens. Docs: cursor.com/docs/models/gemini-4-neon.

tips.author: owickstrom
tips.title: Bombadil 0.8.0: faster browser and TUI fuzzing
tips.tip: Bombadil 0.8.0 (Antithesis's open-source browser and TUI fuzzer) is up to 4x faster for browser fuzzing and 2x for TUIs, with binary compressed traces that cut disk use and IO. Try it with chrome-headless-shell (see the Bombadil docs).

tips.author: EnoReyes
tips.title: Act as the studio exec: give agents outcomes and a budget
tips.tip: Eno made a 57-shot, 5,129-frame 3D short film with Factory's Droids (an unreleased system): his role was giving outcomes and budget while the system designed sets, props, animation, QC, sound and rendering, running Blender on a Mac mini, renting GPUs on Modal and scoring with ElevenLabs. His takeaway: future work looks like one person who knows what they want plus intelligence assembled around goals.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Free course: build your own software factory (Warp Learn)
tips.tip: Warp Learn is a free, hands-on course (taught by @BHolmesDev) that goes from fundamentals to a first automation loop to a full factory with specs, risk assessment and end-to-end verification. Zach's definition: an automation loop in the cloud that orchestrates agents to build better software over time.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Warp Factories: workflows as YAML, dashboards, self-improvement
tips.tip: Define agent workflows as code in YAML; dashboards track code quality, test coverage, regression risk and cost per PR (00:51); a Self-Improvement toggle lets the loop optimize itself (00:58); built-in benchmarking compares configs, subagents and models (01:03).

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Scale human review to the stakes
tips.tip: Agent reviewers, linters and verifiers help but aren't enough; scale human review to the stakes, not to lines of code or PR counts.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Slop is fine when it gets you the outcome
tips.tip: One-shot prompts and vibe coding are fine when they get you the outcome; slop is bad only when it undermines quality, maintainability or teammates' time.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Comment-audit prompt
tips.tip: Ask the agent to categorise every code comment in your codebase (or one section) as Tautology (repeats the code), Excuse (lets a hacky implementation slide), Stale (refers to code that no longer applies) or Decision Record (an important, non-obvious decision). Then: delete tautologies and stale comments, delete excuses and file an issue to fix the hack, and move decision records into ADRs.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Ban comments with a ratchet, then make it a skill
tips.tip: After the cleanup, have the agent add a lint rule banning comments with a ratchet approach (not every comment goes in one PR), create a /delete-comment skill in the repo so you can repeat the process, and estimate how many lines you'll shed.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: Try pstack's /no-comments, or turn it into a lint rule
tips.tip: Run the /no-comments skill from pstack (github.com/cursor/plugins, pstack/skills/no-comments), or better, ask your agent to turn it into a lint rule.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: pstack updates itself; rerun /setup-pstack to change routing
tips.tip: pstack v0.15.46 prunes its skills to be much shorter and adds Gemini 4 Neon as a panel reviewer. It auto-updates for Grok Bot and Cursor users; to change which models handle which role, run /setup-pstack again.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Record hard-won naming decisions in ADRs
tips.tip: When a grilling session settles a naming or data-relationship question (his example ADR: "A Thumbnail Diagram is not a Diagram"), write it up as an ADR; without it the agent would fill the gap with its own assumptions.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: ADRs stop agents re-suggesting explored avenues
tips.tip: ADRs keep agents from repeatedly recommending approaches you've already explored, and let them see the history of surprising decisions after you hand the system off.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Put the 'why' in ADRs, not comments
tips.tip: Comments are a bad store for the why of a codebase, so put it in an ADR instead. Not every piece of code needs one, and don't remove a fence until you know why it was put up.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Only document what won't churn
tips.tip: Low-granularity docs that rarely change (high-level system architecture, one sentence on each package's role) are safe; beyond that, keeping a second copy of the truth tends to slow agents and humans down. Agents that fight doc drift for you have rarely been worth the trouble over a couple of months.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Fork-and-remix prompt for voiced
tips.tip: voiced (github.com/ericzakariasson/voiced) is an open-source dictation and voice-prompting tool powered by Grok voice. To customize it, prompt your agent: "Fork Voiced, read AGENTS.md at its root and follow its first run section, then make this change: …" (e.g. make the pill hot pink, or make the cleanup talk like a pirate).

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Factories vs. agent teams
tips.tip: Treat deploying coding agents as an optimization problem: you can only optimize what you measure, measurement needs standardized data, and that needs a centralized, code-defined factory in the cloud that lets you test different models, harnesses and skills and feed learnings back in. Agent teams that you manage like people lack that measurement loop.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Hands-on software factory course
tips.tip: Warp's team published a hands-on introductory course on learning about and building your own software factory at warp.dev/learn.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Encode the factory declaratively
tips.tip: Define your factory in a declarative, version-controlled language (like Terraform): which agents run, how they're triggered, their workflows and the tools they can use.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Product engineering vs. factory engineering
tips.tip: Building the product and improving the system of agents that builds it are two distinct skill sets; treat factory engineering as its own job.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Record everything agents produce
tips.tip: Centrally record agent conversations, artifacts, videos and screenshots; that record is the raw material for improving the factory.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Keep the inference layer flexible
tips.tip: Run agents in sandboxes for security and repeatability, and support multiple models and agent harnesses, since different tasks need different capabilities.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Online evals score agent output
tips.tip: Have separate agents review and score your coding agents' output as it happens (e.g. flag redundant or unnecessary tests) to catch failure modes.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Self-improvement as PRs
tips.tip: Let agents read the eval scores, find failure patterns, and propose fixes as pull requests against the factory's own definition.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Benchmark on your own tasks
tips.tip: Skip generic leaderboards: build a benchmark from your organization's real past tasks and replay it across models and configurations to weigh quality against cost.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Search flights in chat
tips.tip: Ask for flights in plain words (the demo: "Find nonstop flights from SFO to LAX"); Grok Bot answers with a short pick plus Recommended and Cheapest option cards.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Phone calls from Grok Bot
tips.tip: Grok Bot can make phone calls: call a business, use calls as a tool, hand a call off to you, confirm who it's calling, and show a live transcript.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Per-tool permissions on connector pages
tips.tip: On a connector's page, set each tool to Always allow, Auto-review, Needs approval or Blocked to control exactly what the bot may run without you.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Don't run one chat forever
tips.tip: Using the same bot chat for too long degrades results because it has to re-read the whole chat; spin up fresh bots or split tasks instead.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Install community bots from the Directory
tips.tip: The Grok Bot Directory lists community-built bot templates you can install instead of building from scratch.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Import memory from another assistant
tips.tip: Settings has an "Import memory to Grok Bot" page: click Start import to bring your preferences, context and memories over from another AI assistant.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Sentence-scorer loop for your writing style
tips.tip: To get an agent to write in your style, build a small 'scorer' app where the agent sends you example sentences one at a time and you score them swipe-left style. Plan an article together, work through it sentence by sentence, and let the agent test its own hypotheses about your style and build up a profile over time.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Score one sentence at a time, not pick-the-best
tips.tip: In the scorer, single mode ("score this sentence 1-4") worked far better than multi ("which of these is better"). Reading three options and choosing the best is much harder on your brain than giving fast, vibes-based feedback on one.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Review sentence by sentence
tips.tip: Working sentence by sentence fits the small amount of high-quality working memory people have: instead of judging whether a whole piece flows together, you only judge whether one sentence reads well.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: /vector: six steps to delegate a task to AI
tips.tip: VECTOR is a skill (/vector) for non-developers that walks you through delegating a task to AI in six steps: find workflows AI could help with, give agents the right context, reorder the workflow, and find ways it can improve over time through memory. Planned docs include the /vector skill for building your own workflows, workshop templates for helping people new to AI build theirs, and example prompts.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Plan up front only when rework is costly
tips.tip: Up-front planning with an agent pays off when rework is costly, such as large diffs and features. When rework is cheap, there's not much need for it.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Per-stage subagents cost ~40% more for no real quality gain
tips.tip: On Warp's benchmark, giving each factory stage its own subagent (own context window and computer) averaged $6.27 per task versus $3.84 for one agent running the same stages in a single context window, about 40% more expensive with no meaningful quality gain. The single-agent setup became their default; don't assume subagents pay off until your own benchmark shows it.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Benchmark factory designs by replaying real past tasks
tips.tip: Build a benchmark from real coding tasks your team already completed and replay them through each factory configuration, measuring correctness and cost, instead of picking an agent architecture from opinions online.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Write stage transitions as plain-language conditions
tips.tip: Factory stage transitions don't have to be rigid if/then code. Warp's factory.yaml describes when each stage applies in plain English (e.g. stay in triage while "the cause, scope, or tracking state is not yet known") and lets the agent decide when to move on.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Code mode cut a daily Linear sweep from 245k to 23k tokens
tips.tip: Using Procedural Tool Calling (basically code mode, where the agent writes code that calls the tools) in Factory dropped a daily Linear sweep from 245k tokens to 23k and from 7 minutes to 36 seconds.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Show the model only the fields that drive the decision
tips.tip: Most of the code-mode win comes from making sure the model only sees the Linear fields that matter to its decisions, instead of the giant blobs of JSON tool calls usually return.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Keep the lab's tool defs and system prompt; own the rest
tips.tip: Don't use a lab's harness blindly, but its tool definitions and system prompt are part of how the model was RL'd, so if you depart from them you're on your own. Other parts of the harness, like orchestration, are yours to own.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: If you don't read the code, read the evals
tips.tip: Models are still bad at writing and code-reviewing evals. If you don't read the code an agent writes, at least read its evals.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: Write a skill for your ideal codebase
tips.tip: Matt Pocock is drafting /the-perfect-typescript-codebase, a skill that describes a platonic ideal of a great codebase. After starting a greenfield project with an early version, he called it the best codebase he's ever produced.

tips.author: mattpocockuk
tips.title: A shared chat workspace for agents and developers
tips.tip: Vercel Board is basically a private Slack workspace where your agents and developers work together, and it can sync to Slack channels for observability. Matt Pocock thinks most teams should build their own version from scratch.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: A pstack prompt for gardening your codebase
tips.tip: Run "Use /poteto-mode on this repo", then have it find the mistakes agents and humans keep repeating (git log, past bug fixes, review comments) and make each impossible: architecture first, then types, then a lint whose error names the fix, then a test. Delete comments that restate code (/no-comments), write formal models that replay past concurrency/retry/state-machine bugs (/create-formal-verification-skill) and run them in CI, replace implementation-pinning unit tests with those models plus real DB and e2e tests (keeping security and legal tests), and ship one verifiable PR per step.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Loops = forward pressure + backpressure
tips.tip: Design factory loops with both forward pressure (work starts on its own) and backpressure (agents keep iterating against quality checks) so output reaches a high bar before a human reviews it.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Plan before agents build
tips.tip: Bring back architecture reviews and sprint-style planning before agents write code: about 30 minutes of alignment up front can save hours of review and rework later.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Size planning by expected pain
tips.tip: Don't over-plan. Weigh expected pain (chance you'll have to redo it × how painful the change is): a two-sentence prompt is fine for low-stakes work, while core database changes deserve detailed schemas up front.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Align visually, not with walls of text
tips.tip: Have agents produce visual artifacts such as HTML mockups, charts or tables instead of long text, so humans can quickly understand and agree on a design, before the build or after.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Give agents a way to test their own work
tips.tip: Let agents run the app where it actually lives and check the result with screenshots, a browser, video or cURL. For a mobile app, give them a sandbox where they can build, run and see what happened.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Fight slop with deterministic tools
tips.tip: Don't rely only on AI reviewing AI. Strict linters, type checkers and custom lint rules stop agents from merging known-bad patterns every time.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Slop is a tool
tips.tip: Unreviewed, imperfect output is fine where stakes are low: quick prototypes, side projects, or experiments kept behind feature flags.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Let models run experiments
tips.tip: Connect agents to your feature-flag and A/B testing tools (the slide names PostHog and Statsig) so they can try variations and let real metrics pick the winner.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Compound: eval everything, learn from past sessions
tips.tip: Run evals on everything and feed lessons from past sessions back into the system so the factory gets better over time.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: Unify your forge
tips.tip: Keep designs, decisions and docs in one source of truth (such as GitHub) instead of scattered Slack threads and docs, so humans and agents share the same context.

tips.author: dexhorthy
tips.title: You can't buy a factory
tips.tip: A software factory is a way of working, not a product. You can buy infrastructure, but you still have to tune the rules and governance to your own codebase and team.

tips.author: EnoReyes
tips.title: One prompt that specifies the whole job
tips.tip: Spell out the whole job in one prompt: data source, business logic, output, schedule and notification. The demo prompt: "Build us a compensation tracker. Pull our employees straight from the Rippling API, work out what each person is owed by month in their own currency, and tie it all out across our systems. Publish it as a web app, run it daily at 7am, and once the checks pass, Slack me what changed."

tips.author: EnoReyes
tips.title: Make the agent tie out numbers against the source system
tips.tip: Ask the agent to "tie out" its results across systems. In the demo it writes a check like assert ledger.total() == rippling.total() so the generated numbers are verified against the source of truth instead of reviewed by hand.

tips.author: EnoReyes
tips.title: Automate the run, keep a one-click human approval
tips.tip: Let the scheduled agent pull data, detect changes, run its checks and send a Slack summary, then stop at one human step: the pay run waits for an Approve click once every check has passed.

tips.author: poteto
tips.title: /reframe skill in pstack
tips.tip: "You can only prompt what you can imagine." pstack has a new /reframe skill for when you know what you want but struggle to put it into words; it pairs well with /sharpen. Plugin page: https://x.ai/bot/plugin/9717366

tips.author: Baconbrix
tips.title: Prompt: find and claim your unclaimed money
tips.tip: Prompt Grok Bot: "search for me in my state's official unclaimed money list, then every other state I've lived in. Show me what you find and submit a claim." It found $315.73 for him.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Edit your community listing on grok-bot.directory
tips.tip: Sign in to grok-bot.directory with GitHub (the account that submitted the app), open your submissions and hit Edit to change its name, description, logo and website. A new name or description reruns the security check, so the listing is hidden for a few minutes. If the app isn't in your list, claim it from its page first.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Refresh re-reads plugin.json; set displayName
tips.tip: The directory doesn't pull changes on its own: Refresh in your submissions re-reads your repo's plugin.json and follows renames and moves. To show a friendlier name (e.g. "PR Genie"), add displayName to plugin.json and hit Refresh.

tips.author: ericzakariasson
tips.title: Official apps: edit the marketplace's .cursor-plugin/plugin.json
tips.tip: Official apps mirror the marketplace catalog and can't be claimed on the directory. The marketplace reads .cursor-plugin/plugin.json, not .grok-plugin/plugin.json, so change the description there; it syncs to the directory overnight.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Define your factory in shared code
tips.tip: Don't keep coding-agent setup in someone's head or on one laptop. Define the agents, their roles, skills, triggers and workflow in shared code so the factory is versioned: test a change on a branch, see what changed, roll back if it gets worse. An agent can even spot a recurring failure and propose a change to the factory definition. Aim for a system you can improve, not a perfect day-one config.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: What counts as a software factory
tips.tip: Agent swarms, shared skills and collections of automations can be useful, but a software factory is a code-defined, closed-loop system that runs coding agents, measures how they perform and improves them over time. Declarative beats imperative: define the system in code so you can test, measure and improve it.

tips.author: zachlloydtweets
tips.title: Treat agent deployment as an optimization problem
tips.tip: Frame the goal as securely deploying coding agents to maximize throughput and quality at minimum cost. That chain forces the design: optimizing needs measurement, measurement needs reliable standardized data, that needs centralization, so move agents to the cloud, define the factory in code, keep it open to try different models, harnesses and skills, and feed what you learn back in.

sources.title: All Code Is Slop (Except Mine), Lauren Tan, SpaceXSI (AIE Code talk)
sources.author: poteto
sources.summary: Lauren Tan (@poteto) on scaling Grok Bot's coding agents into a high-trust "software factory". Agents learn from their environment, so remove bad patterns, ban nuanced APIs, and replace prose instructions and code comments with strict architectural boundaries and lint rules. Spend most agent effort on programmatic verification (custom app CLIs, formal proofs, property-based UI tests) so agents verify their own work before human review. Results shown: 10,926 PRs merged in October (of 23,310 total), 19 desktop releases a month with a median 23 hours between releases, a revert rate steady at 0.47%, and comments cut from 65,824 to 1,227 while lint rules grew to 169.

sources.title: LIVE: Writing code that doesn't suck with the creators of Pi (with @badlogicgames and @mitsuhiko)
sources.author: mattpocockuk
sources.summary: Matt Pocock talks with Armin Ronacher (@mitsuhiko) and Mario Zechner (@badlogicgames), the creators of Pi, about where coding agents help and where they don't. Agents are strong tactically (fast code, reliable bug triage) but weak at system design, architecture and ambiguous problems. Use the time agents save on drudgery for quality rather than more features, and keep humans on domain knowledge, trade-offs and oversight.

sources.title: How to fix the code review bottleneck (full walkthrough), @BHolmesDev
sources.author: zachlloydtweets
sources.summary: Ben Holmes (@BHolmesDev) fixes the code review bottleneck in three stages using Warp Factories: an isolated agent-to-agent review loop, end-to-end verification in a sandbox with recorded video, and an automated merge-risk assessment added to the PR description, so humans see polished, verified PRs with a risk summary. In a Warp benchmark shown, an independent reviewer averaged $12.02 and 71.1% correctness vs $4.82 and 68.6% for self-review.
sources.note: Recommended by @zachlloydtweets for anyone thinking about verification and risk assessment in a software factory.

sources.title: Watch me work: building a 21,000-line PR with /grill-with-docs and /retro
sources.author: mattpocockuk
sources.summary: Matt Pocock builds a thumbnail-editor feature for his Course Video Manager app with Claude Code in VS Code. He aligns with the agent first (/grill-with-docs), pins down domain language in GLOSSARY.md plus an ADR, compacts the planning chat into a spec and tickets, runs /implement-spec to get one large PR, then runs /retro so the agent reviews its own work against project standards (it flags ignored rules, too many comments, and a PR too big to review) and splits it into smaller stacked PRs that he reviews and merges one at a time. Matt also offers a free email course on his skills (aihero.dev/skills/subscribe).

sources.title: The Home Repo pattern: working with agents across multiple repos
sources.author: mattpocockuk
sources.summary: Keep one central Home Repo holding all agent skills, tooling, docs and config, always run agent sessions from it, and let it reach into your other repos, so capabilities stay in sync across the team.

sources.title: /animatic skill preview: videos instead of walls of markdown
sources.author: mattpocockuk
sources.summary: Work-in-progress skill that turns a PR into a short narrated video so humans can review agent PRs faster.

sources.title: Emergent Behaviors with Gabe Orlanski, creator of SlopCodeBench: AI That Works #81 (X broadcast)
sources.author: dexhorthy
sources.summary: @dexhorthy hosts Gabe Orlanski (creator of SlopCodeBench, University of Wisconsin) and Vaibhav (@vaibcode, BoundaryML founder). SlopCodeBench tests agents on iterative, multi-checkpoint tasks: agents solve isolated steps but fail to refactor or centralize code as requirements grow, piling on workarounds. Gabe's post "Slop is Moving Up the Stack" adds that agents rewrite libraries instead of using provided ones, and LibraryDesignBench shows agent-designed libraries are hard for other agents to use. Recurring anti-patterns: Go-style (value, error) returns in Python, catch-and-reraise at every layer, and type(x) == T instead of isinstance().

sources.title: 'There will always be alpha in reviewing something': No Slop Manifesto talk excerpt (via @aiDotEngineer)
sources.author: dexhorthy
sources.summary: As models improve, shift review from line-by-line code to plans, designs and outcomes; bring your own thinking or you get the same baseline output as everyone. Slop is fine when it gets you to the outcome, bad when it hurts quality, maintainability or teammates' time.
